question: Which of the following is a core function performed by an operating system?

options.text: Allocating and managing hardware resources such as CPU time and memory among running programs
Compiling Java source code into bytecode
Rendering 3D graphics directly without any driver or OS involvement
Physically manufacturing CPU chips

explanation: Resource management - allocating CPU, memory, I/O devices, and storage among competing processes - is one of the operating system's most fundamental responsibilities.

question: True or False: a system call allows a user program to request a privileged service, such as file creation, from the kernel.

options.text: True
False

explanation: System calls are exactly the defined interface through which user-mode programs ask the kernel to perform operations (file I/O, process control, etc.) that require elevated privilege.

question: An embedded system is designed so that only a minimal core (process scheduling, basic IPC, and memory management) runs in privileged kernel mode, while device drivers and file systems run as separate, isolated user-space server processes. Which kernel design philosophy does this describe?

options.text: Monolithic kernel
Microkernel
A kernel with no mode separation at all
A purely layered kernel with no user-space servers

explanation: This is the defining idea of a microkernel: keep the privileged kernel as small as possible and push most services (drivers, file systems) out to user-space processes, improving fault isolation at some cost to communication overhead (message passing between servers).

question: Why is a trap, such as a divide-by-zero exception, considered synchronous with respect to the CPU, while a hardware interrupt (e.g. a disk finishing a read) is considered asynchronous?

options.text: A trap is generated by the currently executing instruction itself at a deterministic point in the instruction stream, whereas a hardware interrupt arrives from an external device at an arbitrary time unrelated to the instruction currently executing
Traps only occur when the system is shutting down
Interrupts can only happen once per program run
There is no real difference - the classification is arbitrary and interchangeable

explanation: A trap is a direct, immediate consequence of the instruction being executed (e.g. dividing by zero), so its timing is tied exactly to that instruction. A hardware interrupt is raised independently by a device whenever it finishes its own operation, with no fixed relationship to whichever instruction the CPU happens to be executing at that moment.

question: In the standard process state model, which transition occurs when a running process issues a blocking I/O request?

options.text: Running -> Ready
Running -> Waiting
Ready -> Waiting
Waiting -> Running

explanation: A process that cannot continue until an I/O operation completes moves out of Running directly into the Waiting (blocked) state, since it cannot usefully use the CPU until the I/O finishes.

question: True or False: in Unix, a parent process and the child process created by fork() share one single copy-on-write set of pages, rather than the child always getting two fully, eagerly duplicated independent copies of every page at the instant of the call.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Most modern Unix-like kernels implement fork() with copy-on-write: parent and child initially share the same physical pages marked read-only, and a private copy of a page is only made at the moment either process actually writes to it.

question: A process calls fork() and then, in the child branch only, calls exec("some_program"). What is the overall effect of this common fork-exec pattern?

options.text: The parent process is destroyed and replaced by the child
A new child process is created, and that child then replaces its own program image with a completely different program, while the original parent continues running unaffected
Both parent and child end up running the exact same code forever
It causes an immediate deadlock between parent and child

explanation: fork() creates a new process (the child) that is initially a duplicate of the parent; calling exec() inside only the child then overlays that child's memory with a new program, which is exactly how shells launch new commands as separate processes without affecting themselves.

question: Why do modern operating systems implement fork() using copy-on-write instead of eagerly copying every page of the parent's address space at fork time?

options.text: Because copy-on-write makes the child process read-only forever

Because eagerly duplicating the full address space is often wasteful - many fork() calls are immediately followed by exec(), discarding the copy - so deferring the actual page copy until a write occurs (if ever) avoids unnecessary work
Because the hardware does not support copying memory at all
Because it guarantees no page faults will ever occur afterward

explanation: Since a large fraction of fork() calls are followed almost immediately by exec() (which discards the duplicated address space anyway), copy-on-write avoids the wasted work of copying pages that will never actually be modified or used by the child, only copying a page lazily if and when it is actually written to.

question: Creating a new thread within an already-running process is generally cheaper (faster, lower overhead) than creating a new process mainly because:

options.text: A new thread requires duplicating the entire address space, just like a process
A new thread reuses the existing process's address space and resources, needing only a new stack, program counter, and register set rather than a full new address space
Threads do not need a program counter
Threads are always created by a different CPU core

explanation: Since a thread shares the code, data, and most resources of its parent process, creating one avoids the expensive work of setting up a brand-new address space that process creation requires.

question: True or False: if one thread suffers a fatal illegal memory access, it can corrupt data relied on by other threads in the same process, because all threads of a process share the same address space.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Because threads of the same process share a single address space, a bug (like writing through a bad pointer) in one thread can corrupt memory that other threads of that same process depend on - unlike separate processes, which are isolated from each other.

question: A threading library maps many user-level threads onto a pool of several kernel-level threads (fewer kernel threads than user threads, but more than one). Which threading model is being used, and what is its main advantage over many-to-one?

options.text: One-to-one; its advantage is using no kernel resources at all
Many-to-many; by using more than one underlying kernel thread, the application can still run on multiple cores in parallel, unlike a many-to-one model which is limited to a single kernel thread
Many-to-one; its advantage is true parallel execution on every core
None of these describe a real threading model

explanation: The many-to-many model multiplexes a (possibly large) number of user-level threads over a smaller but still greater-than-one number of kernel threads, which lets the application exploit multiple cores in parallel while keeping user-level thread creation cheap - something the strict many-to-one model cannot do, since it is bottlenecked on a single kernel thread.

question: On an 8-core machine running a single CPU-bound process that creates 8 threads to parallelize work, which condition is necessary for all 8 threads to actually execute simultaneously on separate cores?

options.text: The threads must be purely user-level threads implemented with a many-to-one model

The threading implementation must map threads to multiple kernel-level (schedulable) threads, e.g. via a one-to-one or many-to-many model, since the OS scheduler can only place kernel-recognized threads onto separate cores
The process must call fork() eight times instead of creating threads
It is impossible for any threads to run in parallel on multiple cores

explanation: Because the OS scheduler only schedules kernel-level threads onto cores, true simultaneous multicore execution requires enough underlying kernel threads to back the application's user threads - a many-to-one model maps everything onto a single kernel thread, which can only ever run on one core at a time regardless of how many user-level threads exist.

question: Which CPU scheduling criterion measures the time from when a request/process is submitted until the first response is produced (not until it fully completes)?

options.text: Turnaround time
Waiting time
Response time
Throughput

explanation: Response time specifically measures the delay before the system starts responding, which is especially important for interactive, time-sharing systems - it is distinct from turnaround time, which measures time until full completion.

question: True or False: Round Robin scheduling is a preemptive algorithm, since a running process can be forcibly switched out once its time quantum expires.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Round Robin forcibly interrupts the currently running process when its allotted time quantum runs out and moves it to the back of the ready queue, which is the defining trait of a preemptive algorithm.

question: Three processes P1, P2, P3 arrive at time 0 with CPU burst times 6, 2, and 4 respectively. Using non-preemptive Shortest Job First (SJF), what is P1's waiting time?
explanation: SJF with all arriving at time 0 runs shortest burst first: P2 (2) runs 0-2, P3 (4) runs 2-6, P1 (6) runs 6-12. P1 must wait for both P2 and P3 to finish first, so its waiting time is 2 + 4 = 6.

question: Compare preemptive Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) with priority scheduling that uses aging. Which statement correctly describes a tradeoff between them?

options.text: SRTF requires no knowledge of burst times at all, while aging-based priority scheduling does

SRTF can minimize average waiting time but may starve long processes if short processes keep arriving, whereas aging-based priority scheduling directly addresses starvation by gradually raising the priority of processes that have waited a long time
Priority scheduling with aging can never prevent starvation under any configuration
SRTF and priority scheduling with aging are mathematically identical algorithms

explanation: SRTF constantly preempts the running process in favor of a shorter one, which minimizes average waiting time in the general case but offers no inherent protection against a long process being perpetually preempted by a stream of short arrivals; aging deliberately boosts a waiting process's priority over time specifically to guarantee it eventually gets scheduled, directly targeting the starvation problem that plain priority scheduling (and SRTF) can suffer from.

question: What is the main purpose of a lock (mutex) around a section of code?

options.text: To make the code run faster by skipping validation
To ensure that only one thread at a time can execute that section (the critical section), preventing concurrent access to shared data
To permanently prevent any thread from ever accessing that code
To allocate more memory to the thread holding it

explanation: A lock enforces mutual exclusion: whichever thread acquires it first proceeds through the critical section alone, while any other thread attempting to acquire the same lock must wait until it is released.

question: True or False: busy waiting (a spinlock) wastes CPU cycles because a thread repeatedly checks a condition in a loop instead of being put to sleep until the condition becomes true.

options.text: True
False

explanation: A spinlock keeps the waiting thread actively running (checking the lock over and over), consuming CPU time that could otherwise be given to other threads, unlike a blocking wait where the thread is suspended until signaled.

question: In Peterson's solution for two processes P0 and P1, each process sets its own flag[i] = true and sets turn = the other process's index before entering its while-loop wait condition. What is the purpose of also checking the other process's flag in that while-loop condition (not just the turn variable)?

options.text: It has no real purpose and could be removed safely

Checking the other process's flag ensures mutual exclusion holds even if both processes attempt to enter at nearly the same time, since turn alone only resolves which process goes second when both are actually interested in entering
It guarantees the algorithm works correctly on any number of processes, not just two
It is only used to improve performance, not correctness

explanation: Peterson's solution needs both flag[] (declaring interest) and turn (breaking ties) together: flag[] lets a process detect if the other is even interested in entering, while turn resolves simultaneous interest - using either variable alone is insufficient to guarantee the mutual exclusion and bounded-waiting properties.

question: Thread A acquires semaphore S1 then blocks waiting to acquire S2. Thread B has already acquired S2 and now blocks waiting to acquire S1. What situation has been created, and what general principle, if followed, would have prevented it?

options.text: This is normal, correct, deadlock-free behavior

A deadlock has been created because each thread holds a resource the other needs and waits in a circular fashion; always acquiring multiple locks/semaphores in a consistent, agreed-upon global order across all threads would have prevented this circular wait
This situation is called starvation, not deadlock, and is harmless
It can be resolved automatically without any code changes because semaphores self-correct

explanation: This is a classic two-resource deadlock caused by acquiring the same two semaphores in opposite orders in two different threads, satisfying circular wait; imposing and following a strict, consistent global lock-ordering convention for acquiring multiple synchronization primitives eliminates the possibility of this kind of circular wait.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four necessary (Coffman) conditions for deadlock?

options.text: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
Preemption allowed on any resource at any time
Circular wait

explanation: The actual fourth condition is "no preemption" (resources cannot be forcibly taken away) - the option as stated (preemption always allowed) is the opposite of a necessary condition and would actually help prevent deadlock, not cause it.

question: True or False: all four Coffman conditions (mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait) must hold simultaneously for a deadlock to be possible.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Deadlock requires every one of the four conditions to be present at once; negating even a single one of them (as prevention strategies do) makes deadlock impossible in that system.

question: In a resource-allocation graph where some resource types have MULTIPLE instances, a cycle is found in the graph. What can be correctly concluded?

options.text: The cycle definitively proves a deadlock exists, exactly as it would with single-instance resources

The cycle is a necessary but not sufficient condition for deadlock - it is still possible for all processes in the cycle to eventually complete if a resource instance held by a process outside the cycle becomes available and is granted to break the chain
The cycle proves the resource allocation graph was drawn incorrectly
The cycle can be entirely ignored whenever multiple-instance resources exist

explanation: With single-instance resources, any cycle guarantees deadlock, but when a resource type has multiple instances, a cycle only means deadlock is possible - the processes could still proceed if some other, uninvolved process releases an instance of the needed resource, breaking the circular dependency.

question: The Banker's Algorithm declares a system to be in a 'safe state' when a particular condition holds. What is that condition?

options.text: Every process currently holds its full maximum resource claim already

There exists at least one ordering (safe sequence) of all processes such that each process's remaining maximum need can be satisfied using currently available resources plus the resources already held by processes finishing earlier in that sequence
No process is allowed to ever request any more resources
The total number of resources in the system is infinite

explanation: A safe state means a safe sequence exists: processes can be ordered so that, one by one, each can obtain enough resources to finish and release everything it holds, letting the next process in the sequence proceed - this guarantees the system can always avoid deadlock no matter what (safe) requests come next.

question: What is the difference between a logical (virtual) address and a physical address?

options.text: They are always identical numbers in every system
A logical address is generated by the CPU as seen by a running program, while a physical address is the actual location in RAM, with the Memory Management Unit (MMU) translating between the two
A physical address is only used while debugging
A logical address is used only by the hard disk, never by the CPU

explanation: Programs operate on logical addresses within their own address space; the MMU hardware translates each logical address to the corresponding physical address in actual RAM, enabling techniques like paging and address space isolation.

question: True or False: paging can still suffer from internal fragmentation, because a process's last page is often not completely filled with useful data.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Even though paging eliminates external fragmentation, a process's size is rarely an exact multiple of the page size, so the final (partially used) page wastes some space inside the frame - that wasted space is internal fragmentation.

question: A system uses a page size of 4 KB (4096 bytes) and a logical address is represented in 20 bits total. If the offset field needs 12 bits (since 2^12 = 4096), how many bits remain for the page number field, and how many distinct pages can the address space contain?

options.text: 8 bits remain, allowing 256 pages
12 bits remain, allowing 4096 pages
20 bits remain, allowing 1,048,576 pages
4 bits remain, allowing 16 pages

explanation: 20 total bits - 12 offset bits = 8 bits left for the page number, and 2^8 = 256 distinct pages can be addressed.

question: In dynamic (variable-partition) contiguous memory allocation, "best fit" allocates the smallest free block that is still large enough for the request, while "first fit" allocates the first free block found that is large enough. What is a notable downside of consistently using best fit compared to first fit?

options.text: Best fit is always slower to search and also tends to leave many tiny, hard-to-reuse leftover fragments, since it deliberately picks the tightest-fitting block, generating small unusable remainders
Best fit never leaves any fragmentation at all, unlike first fit
Best fit always allocates memory faster than first fit in every case
Best fit cannot be implemented for any real workload

explanation: Because best fit searches for (and leaves) the smallest possible leftover space, it tends to generate many very small fragments that are too small to satisfy future requests, whereas first fit is simpler/faster to search but may leave larger, somewhat more usable leftover blocks.

question: What triggers a page fault?

options.text: A process explicitly calls the exit() system call
A running process references a page that is not currently resident in physical memory
The CPU scheduler switches to a new process
A file is deleted from disk

explanation: A page fault is the hardware/OS mechanism that activates specifically when a memory reference maps to a page marked "not present" in the page table, requiring the OS to fetch it from secondary storage.

question: True or False: Belady's anomaly, where increasing the number of available frames can increase the page-fault count, can occur with FIFO page replacement.

options.text: True
False

explanation: FIFO is a known example of an algorithm exhibiting Belady's anomaly for certain reference strings - it is not a 'stack algorithm' like LRU or optimal replacement, both of which are guaranteed to never get worse as frames increase.

question: For the page reference string 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4 with exactly 3 available frames, using the LRU page replacement algorithm, how many page faults occur in total?
explanation: Tracing LRU with 3 frames: 7(F,[7]) 0(F,[7,0]) 1(F,[7,0,1]) 2(F, evict 7 ->[0,1,2]) 0(hit,[1,2,0]) 3(F, evict 1->[2,0,3]) 0(hit,[2,3,0]) 4(F, evict 2->[3,0,4]). Faults occur on 7,0,1,2,3,4 = 6 faults total (the two references to 0 after it was already loaded are hits).

question: As the operating system increases the degree of multiprogramming (the number of concurrently resident processes) beyond a certain point without adding more physical frames, overall CPU utilization starts to drop sharply instead of rising. What phenomenon does this describe, and why does it happen?

options.text: Starvation, because lower-priority processes are denied the CPU forever

Thrashing, because each process has too few frames to hold its working set, causing continuous page faults; the CPU spends most of its time servicing faults (paging) instead of executing instructions, so utilization collapses even though more processes are "running"
Deadlock, because all processes are waiting on each other's resources
Internal fragmentation, because too many small blocks are wasted inside pages

explanation: This is the classic thrashing curve: beyond the point where there are enough frames for every active process's working set, adding more processes just increases competition for the same fixed frames, so processes constantly fault each other's pages out, and the system spends nearly all its time paging rather than computing - utilization drops even as "concurrency" rises.

question: Which of the following is typically stored as part of a file's metadata/attributes (not as part of its actual data content)?

options.text: The file's creation timestamp and size
Every byte of text inside the file
The exact pixel values of an image file's content
The source code of the application that created the file

explanation: File attributes like name, size, type, owner, permissions, and timestamps describe the file but are stored separately from the file's actual data content, often in the directory entry or inode.

question: True or False: indexed allocation allows a file system to directly access any block of a file via an index/inode structure, without having to sequentially traverse a chain of pointers from the start of the file.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Because an index block (or inode) stores direct pointers to every data block of the file, the file system can jump straight to any block's pointer, unlike linked allocation which must follow pointers one block at a time from the beginning.

question: A file system needs to efficiently support both small files (a few blocks) and very large files (potentially gigabytes), without wasting huge amounts of index-block space on small files or being unable to represent huge files. Which real-world approach, used by traditional Unix inodes, addresses this?

options.text: Using only a single, fixed-size index block for every file regardless of size, no matter how large the file grows

A mixed/multilevel scheme: the inode holds a few direct block pointers for small files, plus single, double, and triple indirect pointers that point to blocks of further pointers, scaling index capacity with file size
Always using pure contiguous allocation for every file, regardless of size
Storing the entire file inside the directory entry itself

explanation: Classic Unix inodes combine a small number of direct pointers (fast access for small files, no wasted index overhead) with indirect, double-indirect, and triple-indirect pointers that reference blocks full of further pointers, letting a single inode scale from tiny files up to very large ones without a fixed, wasteful index size.

question: A file is accessed almost exclusively via random reads/writes to arbitrary offsets scattered throughout its content (not sequential reading from start to end). Which allocation method is LEAST suitable for this access pattern, and why?

options.text: Indexed allocation, because its index block makes random access slower than sequential access
Linked allocation, because reaching an arbitrary block still requires sequentially following pointers from the first block, making random access to block k cost O(k) pointer hops
Contiguous allocation, because it cannot support reading any block except the first one
All three methods perform identically for random access patterns

explanation: Linked allocation stores only a "next block" pointer per block, so reaching an arbitrary block n blocks into the file requires traversing n pointers sequentially from the start - this makes it the weakest choice for random-access-heavy workloads, unlike indexed allocation (direct lookup via the index) or contiguous allocation (direct offset arithmetic).
